title: Felix and the Wardrobe
premise: Emrys Marchetti, once a celebrated restaurant critic, has lost her sense of taste and drifts through a life she no longer claims as her own. When a radio plays a song that was written only for her—by Felix, the love of her life who died before he could record it—she realizes someone is alive who knew him, and that her years of silence have been a kind of theft from herself. Following the song's thread, she uncovers Felix's hidden family: a sister, a nephew, a wardrobe in his old boarding house filled with everything he never sent her. To say goodbye properly, out loud, she must finally choose truth over the comfortable lie of her invisibility—and the ending finds her tasting food again at a table full of strangers who have become her own.
about_author: M. M. Blackwood is the pen name of a former line cook turned essayist who spent a decade writing about other people's kitchens before writing about grief. They live above a bakery they refuse to name, on the theory that some things should stay slightly secret.

chapters.title: The Tenant
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. We meet her numb routine: filing reviews for dishes she cannot taste, eating standing up, sleeping in a hotel-like apartment. A small humiliation at work—a younger critic's gushing review read aloud—establishes her invisibility. Emotional beat: quiet self-erasure, almost comfortable.

chapters.title: Static and a Chord
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. Driving home, a late-night radio program plays an unrecorded song—the melody Felix used to hum while cooking, with lyrics she's never heard. She pulls over, shaking. The host credits 'a demo tape, donated anonymously.' Emotional beat: the dead speaking; grief cracked open.

chapters.title: What She Told No One
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV, with flashback to Felix: how they met over a burnt risotto, his habit of composing songs he refused to record, his sudden death eleven years ago and the funeral she left early. Emotional beat: establishing the love and the unfinished goodbye.

chapters.title: The Station That Plays Ghosts
chapters.summary: Emrys visits the community radio station. A young producer, Dev, shows her the anonymous donation log: a box labeled only 'F.' Someone else has been listening too—Dev mentions a woman who calls every time it airs. Emotional beat: first step out of hiding; hope with teeth.

chapters.title: The Caller
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. He plays detective reluctantly, charmed by Emrys's urgency. The caller is traced to a number in the old harbor district. Dev warns Emrys that what she finds may not match the man she remembers. Emotional beat: loyalty to memory vs. hunger for truth begins its argument.

chapters.title: Number Fourteen
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. She finds the address: a crumbling boarding house where Felix lived before her, still run by his landlady's daughter, Rosa. Rosa recognizes the name Marchetti and goes pale—Felix spoke of her. But there is someone else: a teenage boy watching from the stairs. Emotional beat: the past has a body and a doorstep.

chapters.title: The Boy Who Hums
chapters.summary: Alternating POV, introducing Theo, sixteen, Felix's nephew—son of Felix's estranged sister Marisol. Theo inherited the songs without knowing their origin; the demo was his gift to the radio station. He resents this stranger asking questions about 'Uncle F.' Emotional beat: found family knocking on a locked door.

chapters.title: Marisol
chapters.summary: Emrys confronts Marisol, who cut Felix off decades ago over a family debt and a betrayal Emrys never knew about. Marisol accuses Emrys of being the reason Felix never came home. Emotional beat: loyalty vs. truth turns ugly; both women guarding wounds.

chapters.title: The Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. Rosa unlocks Felix's old room, kept untouched: inside the wardrobe, unsent letters, cassette tapes, a jacket, and a photograph of Emrys she never knew was taken. He meant to come back. Emotional beat: devastating tenderness; the goodbye he wrote but never delivered.

chapters.title: Letters, Unsent
chapters.summary: Emrys reads the letters across one long night—his voice alive again, explaining the rift with Marisol, his fear that he'd made Emrys smaller by loving her, his plan to record one album 'for an audience of one.' Emotional beat: grief reorganized into understanding.

chapters.title: Taste of Copper
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. Overwhelmed, she relapses into numbness, skips work, nearly burns her apartment cooking Felix's recipes. A moment of danger—the stove left on—forces her to admit she cannot keep living as a tenant of her own life. Emotional beat: rock bottom disguised as ordinary Tuesday.

chapters.title: Dev's Offer
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. He offers to air the full tape collection as a memorial series, but needs family consent—which means Marisol. He pushes Emrys to reconcile rather than broadcast over Marisol's objection. Emotional beat: the ethical hinge; doing right vs. taking what's hers.

chapters.title: Two Women, One Kitchen
chapters.summary: Emrys cooks for Marisol using Felix's handwritten recipe cards from the wardrobe. Mid-meal, Marisol finally tastes it and breaks—revealing the real betrayal: Felix took the blame for something Theo's father did. Emotional beat: bitterness dissolving; food as language when words fail.

chapters.title: What Felix Carried
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV, flashback. Her version of the family rupture, and her guilt at letting Felix die unforgiven. She gives Emrys the last letter—the one addressed to 'whoever loved him after me.' Emotional beat: two kinds of survivor recognizing each other.

chapters.title: Theo's Tape
chapters.summary: Emrys and Theo listen together to the final cassette: Felix singing a song written for a child not yet born—Theo. Theo, who thought he invented the melodies, learns they were lullabies meant for him. Emotional beat: inheritance; the boy receives his legacy.

chapters.title: Consent
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. The family gathers—Rosa, Dev, Marisol, Theo—to decide about the broadcast. Marisol consents, on one condition: Emrys must speak on air, say goodbye in her own voice, not hide behind Felix's tapes. Emotional beat: the cost of the goodbye named aloud.

chapters.title: Rehearsal for Goodbye
chapters.summary: Emrys tries and fails repeatedly to write what she'll say; drafts litter the floor. Theo helps her, teaching her the chords so she can play along live. Emotional beat: fear of performing grief; intimacy growing between the found family.

chapters.title: On Air
chapters.summary: Climax. Live broadcast: the tapes play, and then Emrys speaks—naming Felix, naming her silence, saying goodbye out loud, thanking the strangers who became hers. Listeners call in with their own unsaid goodbyes. Emotional beat: catharsis; the private grief made communal.

chapters.title: Aftertaste
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. Days later, at Rosa's table, Emrys eats Marisol's stew and tastes it—fully, shockingly, salt and smoke and all. She weeps into the bowl. Emotional beat: resurrection of the senses; grief metabolized into appetite.

chapters.title: The Review
chapters.summary: Emrys returns to work and writes her last review—not of a restaurant, but of the meal at Number Fourteen, published under her real name with her story attached. Her editor calls it unpublishable; she publishes it herself. Emotional beat: claiming authorship of her own life.

chapters.title: Keys
chapters.summary: Rosa offers Emrys Felix's old room; instead, Emrys and Theo clear out the wardrobe together, distributing the letters, keeping only the photograph. Marisol hands her a key to the family house. Emotional beat: letting go without erasing; doors opening.

chapters.title: An Audience of More Than One
chapters.summary: Epilogue, spring. A small gathering at the boarding house: Dev records Theo's first song, Marisol cooks, Rosa pours wine, and Emrys raises a glass to Felix—goodbye finished, hello begun. Final image: the empty wardrobe, door open, holding nothing but light. Emotional beat: resolution; found family, fully inhabited.
